steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on exploring differential geometry in neural implicit surfaces. Define the neural implicit problem, describe our framework for approximating SDFs from points, normals and curvatures, the curvature-based sampling, and list our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. The neural implicit problem
2. Our framework: approximating the SDF with a smooth network (SIREN basis)
3. Constraints: Eikonal, interpolation, normals, off-surface points
4. Shape operator alignment
5. Curvature-based sampling during training
6. Closed-form differential geometry of the trained surface
7. Contributions and scope

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Neural implicit problem
- level sets of NNs represent implicit surfaces in \mathbb{R}^{3}, accurate results
- train parameters \theta of f_{\theta}:\mathbb{R}^{3}\to\mathbb{R} so zero-level set f_{\theta}^{-1}(0)=\{p\,|\,f_{\theta}(p)=0\} approximates a desired surface
- terminology: neural implicit function / neural implicit surface

2. Framework
- input: discrete sample of points from ground truth surface S; output: f_{\theta} approximating signed distance function (SDF) of S
- explores differential geometry of implicit surfaces in learning -> assume f_{\theta} smooth
- smooth networks: SIREN, IGR
- we use SIREN as basis (properties suitable for reconstructing signals)

3. Constraints
- input \{p_{i},N_{i}\}: points + normals from possibly unknown S
- SDFs have unit gradient -> Eikonal equation \left\lVert\nabla f_{\theta}\right\rVert=1 in \{p_{i}\}
- f_{\theta}(p_{i})=0 and \left\langle\nabla f_{\theta}(p_{i}),N_{i}\right\rangle=1: interpolate points, align gradient with normals
- extend to off-surface points with SDF approximation (avoid spurious components in f_{\theta}^{-1}(0))

4. Shape operators
- above needs two degrees of differentiability
- "alignments" between shape operator d{\frac{\nabla f_{\theta}}{\left\lVert\nabla f_{\theta}\right\rVert}} of neural surface and dN of S -> one more degree
- shape operators carry intrinsic + extrinsic geometry -> more consistency of geometrical features

5. Sampling
- we have points of S; suppose shape operator known there
- usual: uniform batches -> high probability of points with poor geometric detail -> slow learning
- we propose curvature-based sampling to pick points with important details

6. Trained network
- differential geometry formulas computed analytically from shape operator; formulas given along the text

7. Contributions and scope
- main: global geometric representation in continuous setting with NNs as implicit functions; compact, captures details, robust for shape analysis, efficient (derivatives in closed form)
- method approximating SDF of S by f_{\theta}; input points with normals and curvatures
- loss functional using continuous differential geometry; high fidelity, implicit regularization
- discrete differential geometry of dataset to sample important regions; robust, fast training
- closed-form derivatives to estimate normals, curvatures of point-sampled surface (lies near zero-level set)
- focus on surfaces in \mathbb{R}^{3}; adaptable to n-dimensional manifolds in \mathbb{R}^{n+1}, curves, gray-scale images (graphs of 2D functions)
- neural animation of surfaces: see other work

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Level sets of neural networks have been used to represent implicit surfaces in \mathbb{R}^{3}, and the results are accurate. Here the neural implicit problem is the task of training the parameters \theta of a neural network f_{\theta}:\mathbb{R}^{3}\to\mathbb{R} so that its zero-level set f_{\theta}^{-1}(0)=\{p\,|\,f_{\theta}(p)=0\} approximates a surface we want in \mathbb{R}^{3}. We call f_{\theta} a neural implicit function and f_{\theta}^{-1}(0) a neural implicit surface.

In this work we propose a framework for solving the neural implicit problem. The input is a discrete sample of points from a ground truth surface S, and the output is a neural implicit function f_{\theta} that approximates the signed distance function (SDF) of S. The framework explores the differential geometry of implicit surfaces when learning f_{\theta}. So for simplicity we consider f_{\theta} to be a smooth function. Examples of smooth neural networks are sinusoidal representation networks (SIREN) and implicit geometric regularization (IGR). We use the SIREN architecture as a basis, because it has important properties that are suitable for reconstructing signals.

More specifically, let \{p_{i},N_{i}\} be the input, which is a sample of points and normals from a surface S that is possibly unknown. We look for parameters \theta such that f_{\theta} approximates the SDF of S. SDFs have unit gradient, so we ask f_{\theta} to satisfy the Eikonal equation \left\lVert\nabla f_{\theta}\right\rVert=1 in \{p_{i}\}. We also require the conditions f_{\theta}(p_{i})=0 and \left\langle\nabla f_{\theta}(p_{i}),N_{i}\right\rangle=1, which force the zero-level set of f_{\theta} to interpolate \{p_{i}\} and the gradient to be aligned to the normals N_{i}. Also, to avoid spurious components in f_{\theta}^{-1}(0), we extend these constraints to off-surface points by using a SDF approximation.

These constraints need f_{\theta} to have two degrees of differentiability. We also explore the "alignments" between the shape operator d{\frac{\nabla f_{\theta}}{\left\lVert\nabla f_{\theta}\right\rVert}} of the neural surface f_{\theta}^{-1}(0) and the shape operator dN of S, and this needs one more degree of differentiability of f_{\theta}. The shape operators carry the intrinsic and extrinsic geometry of their surfaces, so asking for their alignment would require more consistency between the geometrical features of f_{\theta}^{-1}(0) and S.

5. Sampling
- we have points of S; suppose shape operator known there
- usual: uniform batches -> high probability of points with poor geometric detail -> slow learning
- we propose curvature-based sampling to pick points with important details

6. Trained network
- differential geometry formulas computed analytically from shape operator; formulas given along the text

7. Contributions and scope
- main: global geometric representation in continuous setting with NNs as implicit functions; compact, captures details, robust for shape analysis, efficient (derivatives in closed form)
- method approximating SDF of S by f_{\theta}; input points with normals and curvatures
- loss functional using continuous differential geometry; high fidelity, implicit regularization
- discrete differential geometry of dataset to sample important regions; robust, fast training
- closed-form derivatives to estimate normals, curvatures of point-sampled surface (lies near zero-level set)
- focus on surfaces in \mathbb{R}^{3}; adaptable to n-dimensional manifolds in \mathbb{R}^{n+1}, curves, gray-scale images (graphs of 2D functions)
- neural animation of surfaces: see other work

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Level sets of neural networks have been used to represent implicit surfaces in \mathbb{R}^{3}, and the results are accurate. Here the neural implicit problem is the task of training the parameters \theta of a neural network f_{\theta}:\mathbb{R}^{3}\to\mathbb{R} so that its zero-level set f_{\theta}^{-1}(0)=\{p\,|\,f_{\theta}(p)=0\} approximates a surface we want in \mathbb{R}^{3}. We call f_{\theta} a neural implicit function and f_{\theta}^{-1}(0) a neural implicit surface.

In this work we propose a framework for solving the neural implicit problem. The input is a discrete sample of points from a ground truth surface S, and the output is a neural implicit function f_{\theta} that approximates the signed distance function (SDF) of S. The framework explores the differential geometry of implicit surfaces when learning f_{\theta}. So for simplicity we consider f_{\theta} to be a smooth function. Examples of smooth neural networks are sinusoidal representation networks (SIREN) and implicit geometric regularization (IGR). We use the SIREN architecture as a basis, because it has important properties that are suitable for reconstructing signals.

More specifically, let \{p_{i},N_{i}\} be the input, which is a sample of points and normals from a surface S that is possibly unknown. We look for parameters \theta such that f_{\theta} approximates the SDF of S. SDFs have unit gradient, so we ask f_{\theta} to satisfy the Eikonal equation \left\lVert\nabla f_{\theta}\right\rVert=1 in \{p_{i}\}. We also require the conditions f_{\theta}(p_{i})=0 and \left\langle\nabla f_{\theta}(p_{i}),N_{i}\right\rangle=1, which force the zero-level set of f_{\theta} to interpolate \{p_{i}\} and the gradient to be aligned to the normals N_{i}. Also, to avoid spurious components in f_{\theta}^{-1}(0), we extend these constraints to off-surface points by using a SDF approximation.

These constraints need f_{\theta} to have two degrees of differentiability. We also explore the "alignments" between the shape operator d{\frac{\nabla f_{\theta}}{\left\lVert\nabla f_{\theta}\right\rVert}} of the neural surface f_{\theta}^{-1}(0) and the shape operator dN of S, and this needs one more degree of differentiability of f_{\theta}. The shape operators carry the intrinsic and extrinsic geometry of their surfaces, so asking for their alignment would require more consistency between the geometrical features of f_{\theta}^{-1}(0) and S.

In practice we have a sample of points of S. Suppose the shape operator is known at these points. When training f_{\theta} it is common to sample batches of points uniformly. But then there is a high probability of picking points that have poor geometric details in their neighborhoods, and this makes the network learn slowly. In this work we propose a sampling based on the curvature, to select points with important geometric details during training.

Once we have a trained neural implicit function f_{\theta}, we can calculate the differential geometry formulas of the corresponding neural implicit surface analytically, since we have its shape operator d{\frac{\nabla f_{\theta}}{\left\lVert\nabla f_{\theta}\right\rVert}}. We give the formulas along with the text.

The main contribution of our work is a global geometric representation in the continuous setting that uses neural networks as implicit functions. The representation is compact and captures geometrical details, and the model is also robust for shape analysis and efficient for computation, since we have its derivatives in closed form. The contributions are:

- A method for approximating the SDF of a surface S by a network f_{\theta}. The input is a sample of points from S (the ground truth) with its normals and curvatures, and the output is the SDF approximation f_{\theta}.

- A loss functional that lets us use tools from continuous differential geometry during the training of the neural implicit function. This gives high fidelity when reconstructing geometric features of the surface and it acts as an implicit regularization.

- During training of the network we use the discrete differential geometry of the dataset (point-sampled surface) to sample important regions. This gives robust and fast training without losing geometrical details.

- We also use the closed-form derivatives of a neural implicit function to estimate differential measures, like normals and curvatures, of the underlying point-sampled surface. This is possible because it lies in a neighborhood of the network zero-level set.

We focus on implicit surfaces in \mathbb{R}^{3} in this work. But the definitions and techniques we describe can easily be adapted to implicit n -dimensional manifolds embedded in \mathbb{R}^{n+1}. In particular they can be extended to curves and gray-scales images (graph of 2D functions). For neural animation of surfaces, see other work.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Level sets of neural networks have been used to represent implicit surfaces in \mathbb{R}^{3} with accurate results. In this context, the neural implicit problem is the task of training the parameters \theta of a neural network f_{\theta}:\mathbb{R}^{3}\to\mathbb{R} such that its zero-level set f_{\theta}^{-1}(0)=\{p\,|\,f_{\theta}(p)=0\} approximates a desired surface in \mathbb{R}^{3}. We say that f_{\theta} is a neural implicit function and that f_{\theta}^{-1}(0) is a neural implicit surface.

In this work, we propose a framework to solve the neural implicit problem. The input is a discrete sample of points from a ground truth surface S, and the output is a neural implicit function f_{\theta} approximating the signed distance function (SDF) of S. The framework explores the differential geometry of implicit surfaces in the learning process of f_{\theta}, so for simplicity we consider f_{\theta} to be a smooth function. Sinusoidal representation networks (SIREN) [1] and implicit geometric regularization (IGR) [2] are examples of smooth neural networks. We adopt the SIREN architecture as a basis, since it has important properties that are suitable for reconstructing signals.

Specifically, let \{p_{i},N_{i}\} be the input composed of a sample of points and normals from a possibly unknown surface S. We look for a set of parameters \theta such that f_{\theta} approximates the SDF of S. Since SDFs have unit gradient, we ask f_{\theta} to satisfy the Eikonal equation \left\lVert\nabla f_{\theta}\right\rVert=1 in \{p_{i}\}. Moreover, we require the conditions f_{\theta}(p_{i})=0 and \left\langle\nabla f_{\theta}(p_{i}),N_{i}\right\rangle=1, which force the zero-level set of f_{\theta} to interpolate \{p_{i}\} and the gradient to be aligned to the normals N_{i}. Additionally, to avoid spurious components in f_{\theta}^{-1}(0), we extend these constraints to off-surface points using a SDF approximation.

The above constraints require two degrees of differentiability of f_{\theta}. We also explore the "alignments" between the shape operator d{\frac{\nabla f_{\theta}}{\left\lVert\nabla f_{\theta}\right\rVert}} of the neural surface f_{\theta}^{-1}(0) and the shape operator dN of S, which requires one more degree of differentiability of f_{\theta}. As the shape operators carry the intrinsic and extrinsic geometry of their surfaces, asking for their alignment requires more consistency between the geometrical features of f_{\theta}^{-1}(0) and S.

In practice, we have a sample of points of S, and we suppose that the shape operator is known at these points. During the training of f_{\theta}, it is common to sample batches of points uniformly. However, there is a high probability of selecting points with poor geometric details in their neighborhoods, which leads to slow learning of the network.

This work proposes a sampling based on the curvature to select points with important geometric details during the training.

With a trained neural implicit function f_{\theta} in hand, we can analytically calculate the differential geometry formulas of the corresponding neural implicit surface, since we have its shape operator d{\frac{\nabla f_{\theta}}{\left\lVert\nabla f_{\theta}\right\rVert}}. We provide the formulas along with the text.

The main contribution of our work is a global geometric representation in the continuous setting using neural networks as implicit functions. Besides being a compact representation that captures geometrical details, this model is robust for shape analysis and efficient for computation, since we have its derivatives in closed form. The contributions can be summarized as follows:

- A method to approximate the SDF of a surface S by a network f_{\theta}. The input of the framework is a sample of points from S (the ground truth) endowed with its normals and curvatures, and the output is the SDF approximation f_{\theta}.

- A loss functional that allows the exploration of tools from continuous differential geometry during the training of the neural implicit function. This provides high fidelity when reconstructing geometric features of the surface and acts as an implicit regularization.

- During the training of the network, we use the discrete differential geometry of the dataset (point-sampled surface) to sample important regions. This provides robust and fast training without losing geometrical details.

- We also use the closed-form derivatives of a neural implicit function to estimate the differential measures, like normals and curvatures, of the underlying point-sampled surface. This is possible since it lies in a neighborhood of the network zero-level set.

In this work, we focus on implicit surfaces in \mathbb{R}^{3}. However, the definitions and techniques that we describe can be easily adapted to the context of implicit n -dimensional manifolds embedded in \mathbb{R}^{n+1}. In particular, they can be extended to curves and gray-scales images (graph of 2D functions). For neural animation of surfaces, see [3].

References:
[1] Sitzmann et al. [2020] Vincent Sitzmann, Julien Martel, Alexander Bergman, David Lindell, and Gordon Wetzstein. Implicit neural representations with periodic activation functions. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems , 33, 2020.
[2] Gropp et al. [2020] Amos Gropp, Lior Yariv, Niv Haim, Matan Atzmon, and Yaron Lipman. Implicit geometric regularization for learning shapes. arXiv preprint arXiv:2002.10099 , 2020.
